title: Ang 488: Farid in Asa
hookLine: love from the heart closes the raga
tomorrow: what if your own mind were the grinding stone?

lines: THE LAST SONG ON THE ALBUM.
cards: People argue about the last song on an album more than the first. It's the one you walk out humming. The raga of Asa runs on for page after page of the Gurus' hymns, then the Bhagats.
And on ang 488, the very last word goes to a Sufi, Shaykh Farid, speaking of Allah and the grave. A Muslim saint closes a raga of the Sikh scripture. So here's the puzzle: why him?

teach.h: LOVE FROM THE HEART IS TRUE.
teach.b: Start with what he says. In paraphrase: those who love from the heart are the true ones.

Those with one thing in the mind and another on the lips are counted false. That's Farid's whole test, and notice what's missing from it: any label at all. No question of which community, which name, which door.
Just this: does the inside match the outside? Then he goes on. Those dyed in love for the Lord delight in seeing him; those who forget the Name are a weight on the earth.

teach.h: HOLD ON; THE BODY TURNS TO DUST.
teach.b: In his second hymn he names himself, Shaykh Farid, and tells his dear one to hold on to Allah, because this body will turn to dust. So, the puzzle, solved.

teach.h: SORTED BY THE HEART, NOT THE DOOR.
teach.b: The Granth doesn't sort its singers by the door they came in. It sorts them the way Farid sorts people: is the love real all the way through? Farid says Allah.
The Gurus say Hari, Gobind, the True One. The Granth sets them on the same pages, and Sikhs bow to the whole book.
One small word to tap in his line: dil, the heart. Not the part of you that argues; the part that loves. Asa ends on it.

how: Shaykh Farid's hymns and saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras like the rest of the Granth; in Asa his two hymns are the raga's last, after the other Bhagats.

o: the page where Guru Nanak's hymns open the raga of Gujri
the page where Farid's hymns close the raga of Asa
a page of Kabir's sayings about love and death

s: Farid's hymns in the Granth use the name Allah
in his second hymn he tells his dear one to hold on to Allah.
Farid's test is about which community you belong to
his test is the heart: one thing inside and another on the lips is counted false.
in Farid's line, dil means the thinking mind
dil is the heart, the part that loves.

games.q: you're picking a volunteer lead. one has a perfect resume and talks about it a lot. one says little and keeps showing up. by Farid's test, what are you looking for?
o: whether what each one says matches what they do.
the stronger resume; it proves real commitment.
the quiet one; talking about it means it's fake.
games.why: Farid's test isn't loud or quiet. it's the match: one thing in the mind and another on the lips is what he calls false.

practice: Take a pen and any scrap of paper, and write Farid's test in your own hand: the inside the same as the outside. Set the pen down and leave the words in front of you for the sit, eyes resting on them.
If you'd like to see his lines first, they're on ang 488.

wordCard.voice: Ang 488. The last page of Asa, where Shaykh Farid says the true ones are those who love from the heart.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dilhu muhabbat, love from the heart; Farid's opening on ang 488.

carryVoice: From the heart: Farid's whole test, the inside matching the outside. Fifteen hundred days, and counting.
